```{r options, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 7,
                      fig.height = 4.5, fig.align = "center", dpi = 100)
```

A psychological network is estimated from one sample, and another sample from
the same population would give a somewhat different network. Before an edge is
interpreted or a node is called the most central, the analyst needs to know
whether the result would reappear: whether an edge differs reliably from zero,
whether two nodes can be ranked, and whether the structure survives when part
of the sample is removed or when the sample is split in two. Resampling
answers these questions without distributional assumptions, by re-estimating
the network many times on samples drawn from the data (Epskamp et al., 2018).

This article applies five such diagnostics to one network: bootstrap
confidence intervals for edges and centralities, bootstrap tests of
differences between nodes, the stability of centrality and of edge weights
when cases are dropped, and the agreement of networks estimated on two halves
of the sample. Each diagnostic refits the network with the same estimator, so
the same steps apply to any estimator.

```{r setup}
library(psychnets)
set.seed(1)
```

The diagnostics resample at random, so the seed is set once to make the
results reproducible.

## Data

`SRL_Claude` holds 300 sets of responses to the Motivated Strategies for
Learning Questionnaire generated by a large language model (Claude) in a study
of how such models answer psychological surveys (Saqr, 2025). Its responses
are more internally consistent than human responses, which yields a network
with large edges; it serves here as an example and is not evidence about
students.

- **Nodes:** five construct scores on a scale from 1 to 7: `CSU` (cognitive
  strategy use), `IV` (intrinsic value), `SE` (self-efficacy), `SR`
  (self-regulation) and `TA` (test anxiety).
- **Observations:** one row per respondent; the data are complete.

```{r data}
head(SRL_Claude)
```

Every diagnostic below estimates an EBIC graphical lasso
(`method = "glasso"`), whose edges are partial correlations.

## How precise is each edge?

`net_boot()` draws bootstrap samples of the respondents with replacement,
re-estimates the network on each, and summarizes the distribution of every
edge weight: its mean, its 95% percentile interval, and the proportion of
samples in which the edge was selected. An edge is flagged `significant` when
its interval excludes zero. An applied analysis uses at least 1,000 samples;
200 keep this example short.

```{r boot}
b <- net_boot(SRL_Claude, method = "glasso", n_boot = 200, cores = 1)
b
as.data.frame(b)
```

Eight of the ten edges have intervals that exclude zero and are selected in
every bootstrap sample. The strongest, `CSU`–`SR` (0.73, interval 0.65 to
0.77), is estimated precisely. Two edges are not reliable. `CSU`–`IV` has an
observed weight of 0.002 and an interval from 0 to 0.12, and is selected in
only 55% of the samples; `IV`–`TA` (-0.014, interval -0.13 to 0.02) is
selected in 76%. Neither their presence nor their sign can be interpreted at
this sample size. The plot shows each edge with its interval, ordered by
size:

```{r boot-plot, fig.height = 5}
plot(b)
```

## How precise is each node's centrality?

The same bootstrap samples give intervals for the centrality of each node.

```{r boot-centrality}
as.data.frame(b, what = "centrality")
plot(b, type = "centrality")
```

Self-regulation has the largest strength, 1.95 with an interval from 1.83 to
2.03, which does not overlap with the interval of any other node. Intrinsic
value has the smallest strength (0.99, interval 0.83 to 1.27). The intervals
of cognitive strategy use, self-efficacy and test anxiety overlap, so their
order cannot be read from the intervals alone; the difference test below
addresses it. Expected influence separates the nodes differently,
because self-efficacy and test anxiety have negative expected influence
(-0.37 and -0.33).

## Which nodes can be ranked?

`difference_test()` tests whether two nodes differ in centrality, or two edges
in weight, within the network. For each pair it takes the difference in every
bootstrap sample, forms its percentile interval and a two-sided bootstrap
p-value, and flags the pair when the interval excludes zero. It reads the
samples already stored by `net_boot()`, so nothing is refitted. With ten
pairs, `p_adjust = "BH"` controls the false discovery rate (Benjamini &
Hochberg, 1995).

```{r difference}
difference_test(b, type = "strength", p_adjust = "BH")
```

Nine of the ten pairs differ. Self-regulation is stronger than every other
node (all adjusted p < 0.01), and cognitive strategy use is stronger than
self-efficacy and test anxiety (adjusted p = 0.044 for both). The one pair
that cannot be ordered is self-efficacy and test anxiety: their difference is
-0.12, with an interval from -0.33 to 0.08 and p = 0.26. A report can rank
self-regulation first and intrinsic value last, but should not order
self-efficacy and test anxiety.

## Is the centrality ranking stable when cases are dropped?

`net_stability()` re-estimates the network on random subsets that drop an
increasing proportion of the respondents and correlates the centralities of
each subset with those of the full sample. The correlation-stability
coefficient (CS-coefficient) is the largest proportion of cases that can be
dropped while the correlation stays at or above 0.7 in at least 95% of the
subsets (Epskamp et al., 2018).

```{r stability}
st <- net_stability(SRL_Claude, method = "glasso", iter = 100)
st
```

The CS-coefficient is 0.70 for strength and 0.90 for expected influence. Up
to 70% of the respondents can be dropped and the strength values of the
subsets still correlate at least 0.7 with those of the full sample in 95% of
the subsets. Epskamp et al. (2018) suggest a CS-coefficient of at least 0.25,
and preferably 0.5, before centrality is interpreted; both measures exceed it,
so the centrality order of this network can be reported. The plot shows the
mean correlation at each drop proportion with a band of one standard
deviation and the 0.7 threshold:

```{r stability-plot}
plot(st)
```

## Is the edge structure stable when cases are dropped?

`net_casedrop_reliability()` applies the same case-dropping design to the
edges. At each drop proportion it compares the edge weights of each subset
with those of the full sample through their correlation and through the mean,
median and largest absolute difference. The edge-weight CS-coefficient is
defined as for centrality.

```{r casedrop}
cd <- net_casedrop_reliability(SRL_Claude, method = "glasso", iter = 100)
cd
```

The edge-weight CS-coefficient is 0.90. The correlation between subset and
full-sample edges is 0.999 when 10% of the cases are dropped and still 0.943
when 90% are dropped, so the pattern of edges is preserved even in small
subsets. The absolute differences show the cost in precision: the mean
difference grows from 0.012 at a 10% drop to 0.112 at a 90% drop, and the
largest single-edge difference from 0.028 to 0.261. The pattern is stable, but
individual edge values estimated from a small subsample can be off by more
than 0.2.

```{r casedrop-plot, fig.width = 8, fig.height = 5.5}
plot(cd)
```

## Does the network replicate across halves of the sample?

`net_split_reliability()` divides the sample at random into two halves,
estimates a network on each, and compares the two sets of edges, repeating the
split many times. The result has one row per comparison measure, with its
mean, standard deviation and the 2.5% and 97.5% quantiles across splits.

```{r reliability}
rel <- net_split_reliability(SRL_Claude, method = "glasso", iter = 100)
rel
```

Across 100 splits, the edges of the two halves correlate 0.982 on average,
with 95% of the splits between 0.953 and 0.996. Two independent samples of 150
respondents thus recover nearly the same edge structure. The mean absolute
difference between the halves is 0.064, and the largest single-edge difference
averages 0.142: a typical edge moves by less than 0.1 between halves, while
the least stable edge can move by about 0.14.

```{r reliability-plot, fig.width = 8, fig.height = 5.5}
plot(rel)
```

## Do the diagnostics apply to other estimators?

Each diagnostic refits the network through `psychnet(method = )`, so it
applies to any estimator. With the unregularized partial correlation network:

```{r pcor}
net_casedrop_reliability(SRL_Claude, method = "pcor", iter = 100)
```

The partial correlation network has the same edge-weight CS-coefficient
(0.90), with slightly larger differences than the graphical lasso at every drop
proportion (mean absolute difference 0.139 against 0.112 at a 90% drop),
because no penalty stabilizes the small edges. Each diagnostic also accepts a
set of group networks built with `psychnet(..., group = )` and returns one
result per group.

## When to use which diagnostic

| Question | Verb | Read the result with |
|---|---|---|
| How precise is each edge and centrality? | `net_boot()` | `as.data.frame(b)`, `as.data.frame(b, what = "centrality")`, `plot()` |
| Do two edges or two nodes differ? | `difference_test()` | the returned table, `plot()` |
| Is the centrality order stable when cases are dropped? | `net_stability()` | `as.data.frame(st, what = "cs")`, `as.data.frame(st)`, `plot()` |
| Is the edge structure stable when cases are dropped? | `net_casedrop_reliability()` | the returned table, `plot()` |
| Does the network replicate across halves? | `net_split_reliability()` | the returned table, `plot()` |

- Report bootstrap intervals with every edge that is interpreted, and do not
  interpret edges whose interval includes zero.
- Rank nodes only after the difference test and the CS-coefficient support the
  ranking; a CS-coefficient below 0.25 means that centrality should not be
  interpreted.
- Case-dropping and split-half reliability describe the whole structure;
  bootstrap intervals describe individual edges. A network can be stable as a
  whole while some of its edges are not, as in this example.
- All diagnostics assume that the respondents are independent. Repeated
  measures of the same persons need a resampling scheme that keeps each
  person's observations together.
